summary: From noon until three o’clock darkness covers the land; Jesus cries out to God, says, “It is finished,” commits His spirit to the Father and dies.
key_insight: The only words Mark records from the cross are a question from Psalm 22: “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” Even forsaken, Jesus still calls Him “My God.”
story: From the sixth hour until the ninth hour, from noon until about three in the afternoon, darkness covered the whole land. The sun was darkened. {Lk}

About the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, “Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?” {Mt} that is, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” Some of those who stood by said, “Look, He is calling for Elijah!” {Mk}

After this, knowing that all things were now accomplished, that the Scripture might be fulfilled, Jesus said, “I thirst!” A vessel full of sour wine was sitting there. {Jn} Someone ran, filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed, {Mk} and put it to His mouth. {Jn} The rest said, “Let Him alone; let us see if Elijah will come to save Him.” {Mt}

When Jesus had received the sour wine, He said, “It is finished!” {Jn} Then He cried out with a loud voice and said, “Father, ‘into Your hands I commit My spirit.’ ” {Lk} And bowing His head, He gave up His spirit. {Jn}
differences: Matthew gives Jesus’ cry as “Eli, Eli”; Mark gives it as “Eloi, Eloi.”
Only John records “I thirst!” and “It is finished!” Only Luke records “Father, ‘into Your hands I commit My spirit.’ ” Matthew and Mark mention a final loud cry without giving its words.
Matthew and Mark say the sponge was put on a reed; John says it was put on hyssop. In Matthew the bystanders say, “Let Him alone”; in Mark the man with the sponge says it.
Luke mentions the torn veil here, together with the darkness and before Jesus’ last cry (Luke 23:45). Matthew and Mark tell of it right after His death.
Each describes the moment of death in his own words: He “yielded up His spirit” (Matthew), “breathed His last” (Mark and Luke), “gave up His spirit” (John).

fit.question: Luke mentions the tearing of the temple veil before Jesus’ last cry. Matthew and Mark place it right after He breathed His last. When was it torn?

points.label: Luke groups the signs
points.text: Luke tells the two signs from heaven together, the darkened sun and the torn veil, and then turns to Jesus’ final words. Luke promised an “orderly account” (Luke 1:3), and he sometimes arranges by subject, as when he tells of John the Baptist’s imprisonment before Jesus’ baptism (Luke 3:19–21).

points.label: The same hour
points.text: All three set the tearing of the veil within the same hours of darkness that ended with Jesus’ death. Matthew and Mark fix it more exactly: it was torn as He died.

fit.note: Luke arranges the signs by subject; Matthew and Mark give the exact moment. Both are true to what happened.
fit.short: Luke groups the two signs from heaven together; Matthew and Mark tie the tearing of the veil to the moment Jesus died.

scene.label: Darkness at noon
scene.text: It was not an eclipse. Passover fell at the full moon, when an eclipse of the sun cannot happen, and an eclipse lasts minutes, not three hours. In Scripture darkness often signals judgment: before the first Passover, darkness covered Egypt for three days (Exodus 10:22), and Amos warned, “I will make the sun go down at noon” (Amos 8:9).

scene.label: A psalm that ends in praise
scene.text: Jesus’ cry is the first line of Psalm 22, a psalm of David that begins in forsakenness and ends in praise, with “all the families of the nations” worshiping the Lord (22:27).

scene.label: Eli and Elijah
scene.text: Eli is Hebrew and Eloi Aramaic for “My God.” Some bystanders heard the name of Elijah, whom Malachi had promised God would send before the great day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5). Whether they misheard or mocked, the Gospels do not say.

scene.label: Sour wine and hyssop
scene.text: The sour wine was probably the cheap, vinegary wine soldiers drank. Psalm 69:21 says, “for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” Hyssop, which John alone mentions, was the plant Israel used to put the blood of the Passover lamb on the doorposts (Exodus 12:22).

scene.label: “It is finished”
scene.text: In Greek this is one word, meaning brought to its end, completed. John used the same word two verses earlier: Jesus knew that all things “were now accomplished” (19:28). The work the Father had given Him was done (John 17:4).

witnesses.matthew: Matthew gives the Hebrew form “Eli,” the words of David’s psalm, and says Jesus “yielded up His spirit.” For Matthew, the Son of David dies with the Scriptures on His lips, even as the bystanders misunderstand Him.
witnesses.mark: Mark records only one saying from the cross, the cry of forsakenness, in the Aramaic Jesus spoke, with a translation for his Gentile readers. In Mark’s stark account the Son whom the Father called “My beloved Son” (1:11) cries out to God in the dark.
witnesses.luke: Luke does not record the cry of forsakenness. He gives Jesus’ last words as a prayer of trust from Psalm 31:5, beginning with “Father,” the same word that opened His first saying from the cross (23:34). In Luke, Jesus dies praying.
witnesses.john: John alone records “I thirst!” and “It is finished!” He stresses that Jesus knew all things were accomplished and spoke to fulfill Scripture. In John, Jesus bows His head and gives up His spirit, as He had said: “No one takes it from Me” (10:18).

seeing.reveals: Jesus entered the darkness of being forsaken by God, bearing the judgment our sin deserved (2 Corinthians 5:21), and He never stopped trusting His Father. He died with His work finished, not cut short.
seeing.living: Because Jesus cried, “Why have You forsaken Me?”, believers in their darkest hours pray to a Savior who has gone further into the dark than they ever will. And because He said, “It is finished,” nothing remains to be added to His work. Rest in it rather than trying to complete it.
seeing.ponder: What are you still trying to add to the work Jesus called finished?

preaching.big_idea: In the darkness the Son was forsaken, and with a loud cry He finished the work.
outline: The cry of the forsaken Son (34)
The loud cry and the last breath (37)
preaching.watch_for: Mark’s Gospel opens with the heavens parting and the Father’s voice: “You are My beloved Son” (1:10–11). Here the sky goes dark and the Son asks why God has forsaken Him. The next verses answer with a torn veil and a soldier’s confession (15:38–39).
